title: Upgrading Kubernetes Worker Nodes
content:
# Upgrading Kubernetes Worker Nodes

This runbook covers upgrading the worker nodes of our Kubernetes (k8s) clusters from one minor version to the next. The managed provider upgrades the control plane; the worker node pools are ours. Budget roughly 45 minutes per pool in staging and 90 minutes per pool in production, and never do two production pools on the same day.

## Prerequisites

- The control plane must already run the target version. Nodes may lag the control plane by up to two minor versions but must never be ahead of it.
- Every workload with more than one replica needs a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB). Without a PDB a drain can evict all replicas of a service at once, which is how the March search outage started.
- Read the upstream changelog for removed APIs. Run `kubent` against the manifests repository and fix any deprecated `apiVersion` fields before you start, not during.
- Announce the maintenance window in #platform at least one working day ahead and pin the message.
- Pause the cluster autoscaler for the pool you are working on. If it is left running it will try to remove the surge nodes as "underutilised" while you are still moving pods onto them.

## Step 1: Create the surge pool

We do not upgrade nodes in place. Instead we create a new pool at the target version with the same machine type, labels and taints as the old one, move the pods across, and delete the old pool.

```
platformctl nodepool create --cluster prod-eu-1 \
  --name workers-v129 --version 1.29.4 --clone-from workers-v128
```

Wait until every new node reports `Ready` and the DaemonSets (log shipper, node exporter, CNI agent) are running on all of them. `kubectl get ds -A` should show desired equal to ready everywhere.

## Step 2: Cordon the old nodes

Cordoning marks a node unschedulable, so the scheduler stops placing new pods there while existing pods keep running:

```
kubectl cordon -l pool=workers-v128
```

Cordon the whole old pool at once. This guarantees that pods evicted in the next step land on the new nodes and not on another old node that will be drained five minutes later.

## Step 3: Drain one node at a time

```
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=10m
```

Drain the old nodes one by one and look at the error-budget dashboard between drains. Wait for the evicted pods to be `Running` and passing readiness checks on the new pool before moving on.

If a drain hangs, it is almost always a PDB that can never be satisfied, for example a deployment whose `minAvailable` equals its replica count. Do not force it. Scale the deployment up by one replica, let the new replica become ready on the new pool, and the drain will continue.

### Stateful workloads

StatefulSets with local volumes (the Redis cache and the search indexers) cannot simply be evicted. For each one, trigger a controlled failover first (`platformctl redis failover` or pause indexing in the admin console), then delete the pod manually and confirm it rebinds its volume on a new node.

### Jobs and CronJobs

Long-running batch jobs are not protected by a PDB. Check `kubectl get jobs -A` for anything started in the last hour and either wait for it or coordinate with the owning team. The nightly database backup job runs at 02:00 UTC; never drain during that window.

## Step 4: Delete the old pool

When the old nodes are empty apart from DaemonSet pods, leave them cordoned for 24 hours. This gives a cheap way back if a problem appears overnight. Then delete the pool:

```
platformctl nodepool delete --cluster prod-eu-1 --name workers-v128
```

Re-enable the cluster autoscaler for the new pool and update the pool name in the cluster inventory file (`clusters/prod-eu-1/pools.yaml`).

## Rollback

Because the old pool is kept for a day, rolling back is the same procedure in reverse: uncordon the old pool, cordon the new one, and drain the new nodes. If the old pool has already been deleted, create a pool at the previous version with `--clone-from` and repeat steps 2 and 3. Record any rollback in the change log with the reason.

## Troubleshooting

### Pods stuck in Terminating

Usually a finalizer that nobody is processing. Look at `metadata.finalizers` on the pod. Only remove a finalizer if you know which controller owns it and that the controller is healthy.

### ImagePullBackOff on new nodes

New nodes start with an empty image cache and pull everything at once, which can hit the registry rate limit. Pre-pull the ten largest images with the warm-up DaemonSet before draining.

### Node NotReady after joining

Check the kubelet logs on the node and the CNI agent pod. A version mismatch between the CNI agent and the new kubelet is the usual cause; the agent version is pinned per pool in `pools.yaml`.

title: Tuning the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler
content:
# Tuning the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler

The cluster autoscaler adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled and removes nodes that stay underutilised. Our defaults are conservative because scale-down churn has caused more pages than slow scale-up ever did.

## Settings we run

| Flag | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `--scale-down-utilization-threshold` | 0.5 | Only nodes under half-used are candidates |
| `--scale-down-unneeded-time` | 15m | Must stay underused for 15 minutes |
| `--scale-down-delay-after-add` | 20m | Avoids flapping after a burst |
| `--expander` | least-waste | Picks the node group that wastes least CPU and memory |
| `--max-node-provision-time` | 12m | Gives up on a stuck node group |

## Common problems

- **Pods pending but no scale-up.** The pod requests more memory than any node group can offer, or a node selector matches no group. The autoscaler logs `NotTriggerScaleUp` with the reason.
- **Nodes never scale down.** A pod with local storage or the `cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false"` annotation pins the node.
- **Cost spikes at night.** Batch CronJobs request large amounts of CPU; give them their own node group with a maximum size.

Per-pool minimum and maximum sizes live in `clusters/<name>/pools.yaml`. Changes go through a normal pull request and are applied by the platform pipeline.

title: PostgreSQL Backup and Restore Runbook
content:
# PostgreSQL Backup and Restore Runbook

This runbook describes how the orders and accounts databases are backed up, how long backups are kept, and how to restore them. It applies to every PostgreSQL cluster tagged `tier=critical`.

## What we take and when

We combine two mechanisms:

1. **A full physical base backup** with `pg_basebackup`, taken nightly at **02:00 UTC** from the streaming replica (never from the primary, to avoid I/O contention during the European evening peak).
2. **Continuous WAL archiving.** Every completed write-ahead log segment is shipped to object storage by `archive_command` within about a minute.

Together they allow point-in-time recovery (PITR): restoring the database to any moment within the retention window, not just to the moment of the last nightly snapshot.

We also take a logical `pg_dump` of each database every Sunday at 04:00 UTC. The logical dump is slower to restore but survives major-version upgrades and is what we hand to analysts for ad hoc work.

## Retention

| Artifact | Kept for | Storage class |
|---|---|---|
| Base backups | 14 days | Standard |
| WAL segments | 14 days | Standard |
| Weekly pg_dump | 12 weeks | Infrequent access |
| Month-end pg_dump | 13 months | Archive |

Retention is enforced by a bucket lifecycle rule, not by the backup job, so a failing job cannot accidentally delete history.

## Monitoring

The backup job writes a success marker with the size and duration of the base backup. Alerts fire when:

- no success marker has appeared for 26 hours;
- the newest archived WAL segment is more than 10 minutes old;
- the base backup is more than 30 percent smaller than the previous one (usually a sign that it backed up the wrong cluster).

The second alert did not exist before the archive incident in OPS-244; the job reported success while WAL shipping had been broken for days.

## Restoring

### Restore to the latest state

1. Provision a new instance from the `postgres-restore` template. Never restore over a running primary.
2. Fetch the newest base backup: `backupctl fetch --cluster orders --latest`.
3. Create `recovery.signal` and set `restore_command` to pull WAL segments from the archive.
4. Start PostgreSQL and watch the log until it reports `archive recovery complete`.
5. Run the smoke checks in `restore/verify.sql` (row counts on the ten largest tables, latest order timestamp).

### Point-in-time restore

Follow the same steps, but also set `recovery_target_time` to the moment just before the bad change, for example `'2024-03-14 09:41:00+00'`, and `recovery_target_action = 'promote'`. Pick the time from the audit log or the application logs, not from memory. If you overshoot, you have to start again from the base backup; you cannot move a recovered cluster backwards.

### Restoring a single table

Restore the whole cluster to a scratch instance using PITR, then copy the table across with `pg_dump -t` and `psql`. Do not attempt partial physical restores.

## Monthly restore test

On the first Tuesday of each month the on-call engineer restores last night's backup of the orders database to a scratch instance, runs the verification queries and records the elapsed time in the restore log. Our target recovery time is under 90 minutes for the orders database; the last three tests took 52, 61 and 58 minutes. A backup that has never been restored is not a backup.

## Encryption and access

Backups are encrypted at rest with a key held in the cloud key management service, separate from the database credentials. Only the backup service account can write to the backup bucket, and only the restore role can read from it. Deleting objects requires a second approver, and the bucket has object lock enabled for the retention period, so even an administrator cannot remove a base backup early.

## How the backup job works

The job runs as a Kubernetes CronJob in the `data-ops` namespace. It:

1. checks that the replica is streaming and less than 60 seconds behind;
2. runs `pg_basebackup` with `--checkpoint=fast` and compression;
3. uploads the result in parts and verifies each part's checksum;
4. writes the success marker only after the upload is verified.

A run normally takes 35 to 45 minutes. If it has not finished by 04:00 UTC it is killed and an alert fires, because a backup still running during the morning peak competes with reporting queries.

## Who to ask

The platform team owns the tooling. For questions about replication settings or unusual recovery scenarios, the external PostgreSQL consultant is listed in the contacts folder.

title: Monitoring Postgres Replication Lag
content:
# Monitoring Postgres Replication Lag

Streaming replicas serve read traffic for reporting and search indexing, so replication lag directly affects how fresh those views are.

## How we measure it

On the primary we read `pg_stat_replication` and report `replay_lag` per replica. On each replica we also export `now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()`, which is more honest when the primary is idle (it grows even when there is nothing to replay, so we suppress it when the primary has no writes).

## Thresholds

- **Warning at 30 seconds** for five minutes: post to #platform-alerts.
- **Page at 120 seconds** for five minutes: the reporting replica is removed from the read pool automatically and the on-call engineer is paged.

## Usual causes

1. Long-running queries on the replica conflicting with vacuum on the primary. We run with `hot_standby_feedback = on` and a 30 second `max_standby_streaming_delay`.
2. A large batch update or index build on the primary generating WAL faster than the replica can apply it.
3. Network saturation during the nightly base backup, which is taken from the replica.

## What not to do

Do not restart a lagging replica to "clear" the lag. It has to replay the same WAL again after the restart and falls further behind.

title: Speeding Up the CI Pipeline
content:
# Speeding Up the CI Pipeline

Our continuous integration (CI) pipeline had crept up to 38 minutes for a typical pull request. These are the changes that brought it back to about 14 minutes, and the rules that keep it there.

## Dependency caching

Every job used to install dependencies from scratch. We now cache the package store keyed on the lockfile hash, with a fallback to the most recent cache for the same branch. A cache hit saves around six minutes per job. If you change the lockfile, the first run on your branch is slow; that is expected.

## Test sharding

The unit suite is split into eight parallel shards balanced by the timing data from the previous run on `main`. Adding a shard is cheap, but more than eight made things slower because of per-job start-up time.

## Flaky test quarantine

A test that fails and then passes on retry is reported as flaky. After three flaky results in a week it is moved to the quarantine suite automatically, which runs but cannot fail the build, and an issue is opened for the owning team. Quarantined tests must be fixed or deleted within two weeks.

## Build runners

CI jobs run on self-hosted build runners. Each runner cleans its workspace after a job, and a nightly job prunes the Docker image cache. Keep build logs at the default verbosity; debug logging on every job is what filled the runner disks in OPS-252.

## Rules

- A CI job must finish in under 15 minutes or be split.
- No network calls to third-party services from unit tests.
- Cache keys must include the lockfile hash.

title: Deploying and Rolling Back Services
content:
# Deploying and Rolling Back Services

Every service is deployed with `shipctl`, which wraps our Kubernetes manifests and the canary analysis.

## Before you deploy

- The change has passed CI on `main`.
- The deployment does not overlap an open incident or a freeze window (see #releases).
- Database migrations are backwards compatible with the currently running version. Deploying code that needs a new column before the migration has run is the classic cause of a failed rollout.

## Deploying

```
shipctl deploy orders-api --version 2024.03.18-2
```

A deploy starts with a 5 percent canary. Canary analysis compares error rate, p99 latency and saturation against the baseline for ten minutes. If all three stay within bounds, `shipctl` promotes the release to 25, 50 and then 100 percent, pausing five minutes at each step. The whole deployment takes about 30 minutes.

While deploying, keep the service dashboard open. You own the deployment until it reaches 100 percent and stays healthy for 15 minutes.

## Rolling back

If canary analysis fails, `shipctl` rolls back automatically and posts the failing metric in #releases. To roll back manually at any stage:

```
shipctl rollback orders-api
```

This returns traffic to the previous release immediately; it does not revert database migrations. After a rollback, open an issue describing what was rolled back and why, and do not redeploy the same version.

## Hotfixes

Hotfixes follow the same process with a shorter canary (five minutes). Skipping the canary entirely needs approval from the incident commander.

title: Postmortem: Checkout Timeouts During the Spring Sale (OPS-217)
content:
# Postmortem: Checkout Timeouts During the Spring Sale (OPS-217)

**Status:** complete. **Severity:** SEV-1. **Incident commander:** Alexandra Quillon. **Ticket:** OPS-217.

## Summary

For 47 minutes on 14 March, between 18:12 and 18:59 UTC, roughly 22 percent of checkout attempts failed. Customers saw "Something went wrong with your payment" and the orders service logged error **E4012** (`PAYMENT_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT`). No payments were double-charged, but about 3,100 orders were abandoned during the spring sale peak.

## Impact

- 22 percent of checkout attempts failed with E4012 at peak.
- Median checkout latency rose from 1.4 s to 9.8 s for requests that did succeed.
- Support received 410 tickets in the following two hours.
- Estimated lost revenue: under review by finance.

## Timeline (UTC)

- **17:55** Release 2024.03.14-3 of `orders-api` is deployed. It raises worker concurrency from 16 to 48 per pod to cope with sale traffic.
- **18:12** First E4012 errors. Alert "checkout error rate above 2 percent" fires.
- **18:19** On-call engineer acknowledges and suspects the payment provider, whose status page reports degraded performance in one region.
- **18:31** Payment provider confirms their side is healthy for our account. Investigation turns to our own services.
- **18:38** Database dashboard shows the orders database connection pool at 100 percent, with requests queueing for a connection for up to 8 seconds.
- **18:44** Decision to roll back release 2024.03.14-3.
- **18:52** Rollback complete. Pool usage drops to 60 percent.
- **18:59** Error rate back below the alert threshold. Incident resolved.

## Root cause

The payment call itself was not slow. Each checkout request first reserves inventory in the orders database and then calls the payment gateway, holding its database connection for the whole call. Tripling worker concurrency tripled the number of connections each pod wanted, but the pool size of 20 per pod was unchanged. Requests queued waiting for a connection, and the time spent queueing counted against the 5 second gateway timeout, so the gateway call was reported as timing out (E4012) even though it never started.

The error code pointed away from the real cause, and the provider's unrelated regional degradation made the wrong theory plausible for twenty minutes.

## What went well

- The alert fired within a minute of the first errors.
- Rollback was fast and clean.
- Payments were idempotent, so retries caused no double charges.

## What went badly

- E4012 is raised for any timeout on the payment path, including time spent waiting for a database connection. The code was misleading.
- There was no alert on connection pool saturation.
- The release was not load tested at sale traffic.

## Detection and response

Detection was good: the checkout error-rate alert fired within a minute. Diagnosis was slow. For almost twenty minutes the responders looked at the payment provider because E4012 names the gateway, and because the provider's status page happened to show an unrelated problem. The database dashboard that showed the saturated connection pool was not linked from the checkout runbook, and nobody thought to open it until 18:38.

The decision to roll back was made six minutes after the pool saturation was spotted. In hindsight, rolling back the most recent deployment should have been the first move: it was the only change in the previous hour, and a rollback is cheap and reversible.

## Customer communication

The status page was updated at 18:27, fifteen minutes after the first errors, with a generic "payments degraded" message. Support was not told that retrying after a few minutes would work, so many customers abandoned their carts instead. From now on the incident commander assigns a communications lead for every SEV-1, and the first status update goes out within ten minutes.

## Action items

| Ticket | Action | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| OPS-219 | Add a retry budget for payment gateway calls and stop counting pool wait time towards the gateway timeout | Payments team |
| OPS-220 | Alert on connection pool usage above 85 percent for 3 minutes | Platform team |
| OPS-221 | Load test every release that changes concurrency, at 2x the previous peak | Orders team |
| OPS-222 | Split E4012 into separate codes for pool wait and gateway timeout | Payments team |

## Lessons

Release the connection before calling a slow external dependency. Treat configuration changes that alter concurrency as risky as code changes.

title: OPS-219: Retry Budget for Payment Gateway Calls
content:
# OPS-219: Retry Budget for Payment Gateway Calls

Follow-up from the checkout postmortem (OPS-217, error E4012). Gateway calls now retry at most twice within a 10 percent retry budget per pod, and connection wait time no longer counts towards the gateway timeout. Merged and deployed 21 March.

title: Incident Report: Internal DNS Resolution Failures (OPS-231)
content:
# Incident Report: Internal DNS Resolution Failures (OPS-231)

**Ticket:** OPS-231. **Severity:** SEV-2. **Duration:** 26 minutes.

## What happened

Between 09:04 and 09:30 UTC on 2 April, services in the `prod-eu-1` cluster intermittently failed to resolve each other's names. Calls between services failed with error **E5003** (`SERVICE_DISCOVERY_FAILED`) and the application logs showed `SERVFAIL` and `i/o timeout` responses from the cluster DNS.

## Cause

CoreDNS runs as two pods with a memory limit of 170 MiB. A new batch service started resolving thousands of external hostnames per second without any client-side caching. CoreDNS cache memory grew until both pods were OOMKilled and restarted repeatedly, and while they restarted every lookup in the cluster failed or timed out.

## Resolution

We raised the CoreDNS memory limit to 512 MiB, scaled it to four replicas and enabled NodeLocal DNSCache so that most lookups are answered on the node. The batch service was fixed to reuse resolved addresses.

## Follow-ups

- OPS-232: alert on CoreDNS restarts and on the rate of SERVFAIL responses.
- OPS-233: add a DNS lookup budget to the service template.
- OPS-234: document how to read CoreDNS metrics in the platform handbook.

title: Incident: Nightly Database Backup Silently Failed for Six Days (OPS-244)
content:
# Incident: Nightly Database Backup Silently Failed for Six Days (OPS-244)

**Ticket:** OPS-244. **Severity:** SEV-2 (no data lost, but the recovery window was at risk).

## What happened

The nightly base backup of the orders database, which runs at 02:00 UTC, kept reporting success from 3 to 9 May. During that time WAL archiving was broken: every call to `archive_command` failed with **E2207** (`ARCHIVE_UPLOAD_DENIED`) after the storage credentials used by the archiver were rotated without updating the replica's secret. The base backups themselves were fine, but point-in-time recovery for those six days would only have been possible to the moment of each nightly backup.

We noticed when disk usage on the replica climbed to 81 percent because unarchived WAL segments were piling up in `pg_wal`.

## Why it was silent

The backup job only checked its own exit code. Nothing checked that WAL segments were reaching object storage.

## Fix

- The archiver secret is now read from the secret store at start-up, so a rotation takes effect on the next restart and fails loudly if the new secret is invalid.
- New alert: the newest archived WAL segment must be less than 10 minutes old.
- The monthly restore test now also performs a point-in-time restore to a random moment in the previous 24 hours.

## Related

The general backup schedule, retention and restore procedure are described in the PostgreSQL backup runbook.

title: Postmortem: Expired TLS Certificate on the Public API (OPS-198)
content:
# Postmortem: Expired TLS Certificate on the Public API (OPS-198)

**Ticket:** OPS-198. **Severity:** SEV-1. **Duration:** 1 hour 12 minutes.

## Summary

On 11 January at 00:00 UTC the TLS certificate for `api.bluefen.example` expired. Every client connecting to the public API over HTTPS failed the handshake. Browsers showed a certificate warning; our SDKs raised error **E4031** (`TLS_HANDSHAKE_FAILED`). Partner integrations that call the API overnight failed for the full duration.

## Why it expired

The certificate for the public API gateway was the last one still issued manually. It had a one-year validity, the renewal reminder went to a mailbox belonging to someone who had left the company, and the calendar entry had been deleted in a clean-up. All other certificates were already renewed automatically.

## Timeline (UTC)

- **00:00** Certificate expires. Synthetic checks start failing but only post to a low-priority channel.
- **00:41** A partner's on-call engineer emails support.
- **00:58** Our on-call engineer is paged by support and confirms the expiry.
- **01:12** A new certificate is issued and installed on the gateway.

## Action items

- Move the gateway certificate to automatic issuance and renewal over ACME, like every other certificate (done).
- Synthetic TLS checks page when a certificate is within 14 days of expiry, and immediately on handshake failure.
- Inventory of every certificate we serve, with its issuer and renewal method, reviewed quarterly.

title: Build Runners Ran Out of Disk Space (OPS-252)
content:
# Build Runners Ran Out of Disk Space (OPS-252)

**Ticket:** OPS-252. **Severity:** SEV-3. **Duration:** about 3 hours of degraded CI.

## What happened

From 10:15 UTC on 22 May, jobs on the self-hosted build runners started failing with **E7100**, our runner agent's code for `no space left on device`. By 11:00 almost every pipeline was red, and merges to `main` were blocked.

## Cause

A change to the shared job template turned on debug logging for every step so that a flaky integration test could be investigated. Each job wrote several gigabytes of logs into the workspace, and the log collector copied them to the runner's local disk before uploading. The nightly Docker prune does not touch that directory, so the disks filled within a few hours.

## Resolution

We reverted the template change, cleared the log directories on all runners, and restarted the runner agents. Pipelines were green again by 13:20.

## Follow-ups

- Log files larger than 200 MB are truncated before upload.
- The runner clean-up job now also removes old log directories.
- Alert when any runner disk is above 80 percent.
- Debug logging can now be enabled for a single job, not for the whole template.

title: Kestrel Project Kickoff
content:
# Kestrel Project Kickoff

**Date:** 4 April. **Attendees:** Katherine Fenwright (product), Elizabeth Marrowby (platform), Jennifer Okereke-Lund (recruiting), Oskar Lindqvell (mobile)

## Goal

Kestrel is the field-notes app for site inspectors. Inspectors often work in basements and rural sites with no signal, so the app must work fully offline and sync later. Kate framed the first release around a single promise: an inspector never loses a note.

## Scope for v1

- Create, edit and photograph notes offline.
- Background sync when a connection returns, with automatic conflict handling for the common cases.
- Export of a site's notes to PDF.

Out of scope for v1: push notifications, shared checklists, tablet layout.

## Staffing

Jen confirmed two open requisitions for mobile engineers, with the first interviews next week. Liz will lend one platform engineer for the sync service for the first two months.

## Risks

- Conflict resolution is the hard part. Kate asked Oskar to write the sync spec before any UI work starts.
- Photo uploads on slow connections may drain batteries; needs measuring on real devices.

## Next steps

- Oskar: offline sync spec, draft in two weeks.
- Kate: interview five inspectors about how they work today.
- Jen: schedule the mobile engineer loops.

title: Q3 Budget Review
content:
# Q3 Budget Review

**Attendees:** William Halvardsen (Finance), Katherine Fenwright (Product), Elizabeth Marrowby (Platform)

## Cloud spend

Bill opened with the numbers: cloud spend is up 18 percent quarter on quarter, against a planned 8 percent. Most of the increase is the new batch workloads and the larger database instances bought ahead of the spring sale. Liz thinks half of it can be clawed back by moving batch jobs to their own autoscaled node group and by downsizing two database replicas that are now idle.

## Headcount

Kate asked to keep the two Kestrel mobile engineer roles in the Q3 plan. Bill agreed on the condition that one of them starts no earlier than August.

## Travel and expenses

Travel spend is on plan. Bill reminded everyone that the expense policy's 30-day receipt deadline is now enforced by the finance portal: late claims are rejected automatically.

## Decisions

- Cloud spend target for Q3: at most 5 percent above Q2.
- Liz to present a savings plan at the next review.
- Both Kestrel roles approved, one deferred to August.

## Action items

- Liz: cloud savings plan by 1 July.
- Bill: send updated budget sheet.
- Kate: confirm hiring timeline with recruiting.

title: Hiring Debrief: Senior SRE Loop
content:
# Hiring Debrief: Senior SRE Loop

**Attendees:** Jennifer Okereke-Lund (recruiting), Alexandra Quillon (hiring manager), Oskar Lindqvell, Nicholas Ventrella (guest interviewer)

Debrief for the senior site reliability engineering role. Candidate names are kept in the applicant tracking system; notes here use letters.

## Candidate A

Strong on Kubernetes operations and on-call experience. Weak system design interview: jumped to tools before understanding the problem. Alex: lean no. Oskar: lean no.

## Candidate B

Excellent incident management interview; walked through a real postmortem and was candid about their own mistake. Good PostgreSQL depth (Nick was impressed by the answer on replication and failover). Coding interview was average. Everyone: yes.

## Decision

Extend an offer to Candidate B at senior level. Jen will prepare the offer and aims to call the candidate on Thursday. Alex will do a sell call about the on-call rotation, which is the most common concern for SRE candidates.

## Process notes

Jen suggested dropping the take-home exercise because two strong candidates withdrew rather than do it. Agreed to replace it with a paired debugging session for the next loop.

title: 1:1 with Alex: Career Goals
content:
# 1:1 with Alex: Career Goals

Monthly 1:1 with Alexandra Quillon.

## On-call

Alex has been incident commander for three of the last four SEV-1s, including the checkout timeouts. It is sustainable for now, but she wants the second senior SRE hire to take half of the commander rotation.

## Growth

Alex wants to move towards a staff engineer role rather than into management. We agreed the most useful evidence would be leading the reliability review of Kestrel's sync service end to end and writing the incident-response training for new on-call engineers.

## Feedback

Her postmortems are the clearest on the team. One thing to improve: decisions made in incident channels do not always reach the people who were not there. She will try a short written summary at the end of each incident.

## Follow-ups

- Me: raise the staff engineer path with Liz.
- Alex: draft the incident-response training outline before the next 1:1.

title: Call Notes: Renewal with Robert Tavistrom
content:
# Call Notes: Renewal with Robert Tavistrom

Call with Bob (Robert Tavistrom, Halden & Crewe Brokers), 20 minutes, about the car policy renewal due on 1 June.

title: Kestrel: Offline Sync Specification
content:
# Kestrel: Offline Sync Specification

**Status:** approved for v1. **Author:** Oskar Lindqvell. **Product:** Katherine Fenwright.

## Problem

Kestrel is used by site inspectors who spend much of their day without a network connection: basements, plant rooms, rural sites. Today they write on paper and retype in the evening. Kestrel must let them create and edit notes with no connection at all, and reconcile everything once a connection returns, without ever losing an inspector's work.

## Goals

- Every edit made offline is eventually stored on the server.
- Two inspectors editing the same note on different devices never silently lose each other's changes.
- Sync runs in the background and does not noticeably drain the battery.

## Non-goals

- Real-time collaborative editing of the same paragraph.
- Syncing between devices directly without the server.

## Data model on the device

Each device holds a local SQLite store with the notes for the sites assigned to the inspector. Every record carries:

- a stable UUID generated on the device;
- a per-field version stamp using a hybrid logical clock (HLC), which combines the device's wall-clock time with a counter so stamps stay ordered even when device clocks drift;
- a `dirty` flag set on any local change.

Deletions are recorded as tombstones, not removed, so that a delete made offline is not undone when an older copy of the note arrives from another device.

## Sync protocol

1. **Push.** The device sends all dirty records in batches of 50, with their field stamps.
2. **Merge on the server.** For each field, the server keeps the value with the higher HLC stamp. This is last-writer-wins per field, not per record, so one inspector changing the title and another adding a measurement both survive.
3. **Pull.** The device asks for every change since its last sync cursor and applies it locally using the same rule.
4. **Acknowledge.** The cursor only advances after the device has committed the pulled changes, so an interrupted sync simply repeats.

## Conflict resolution

Per-field last-writer-wins handles most cases. Two cases need more:

### Free-text body

If two devices edit the body of the same note while both are offline, choosing one silently would lose work. Instead the server keeps both versions: the later one becomes the body and the earlier one is appended as a clearly marked "conflicting edit from <device> at <time>" block. The inspector resolves it by hand. In the field trial this happened on 0.4 percent of notes.

### Delete versus edit

If one device deletes a note and another edits it, the edit wins and the note is restored, with a banner saying it had been deleted elsewhere. Losing a deletion is cheaper than losing an inspection finding.

## Attachments

Photos are stored locally and uploaded separately from note data, only on Wi-Fi by default and in the background task window the operating system allows. A note references its photos by content hash, so a photo uploaded twice is stored once. If a photo has not uploaded yet, the server shows a placeholder to other users.

## Failure handling

- Requests are retried with exponential backoff up to one hour.
- If the server rejects a record (for example a validation error), it is moved to a local "needs attention" list instead of blocking the rest of the queue.
- A sync log on the device, exportable from the settings screen, records the last 500 sync events for support.

## Sync service API

The server exposes two endpoints to the app, both authenticated with the inspector's session token:

- `POST /sync/push` accepts up to 50 records and returns, for each, either the merged field stamps or a rejection reason.
- `GET /sync/pull?cursor=<c>` returns up to 200 changes after the cursor and the next cursor.

Both endpoints are idempotent: pushing the same batch twice produces the same result, which makes retries after a dropped connection safe. The sync service writes to its own PostgreSQL database and publishes every accepted change on the change stream for search indexing and the supervisor dashboard.

## Metrics

- Share of notes with an unresolved conflict block, target under 1 percent.
- Median time from reconnect to fully synced, target under 60 seconds.
- Battery used by sync per inspection day, target under 3 percent.

## Open questions

- Whether shared checklists (v2) need a different merge rule, since list order matters.
- How long tombstones must be kept before they can be purged safely.

title: Kestrel Push Notifications
content:
# Kestrel Push Notifications

**Status:** draft for v2. Out of scope for the first Kestrel release.

## Purpose

Tell inspectors when something they care about changes: a site is newly assigned to them, a supervisor comments on a note, or a sync has been stuck for more than a day.

## Delivery

Notifications are sent through the platform push services for iOS and Android. The server stores one device token per installation and removes tokens that the push service reports as invalid.

## Rules

- Quiet hours from 20:00 to 07:00 in the inspector's time zone; anything non-urgent is held until morning.
- At most five notifications per inspector per day; the rest are grouped into a daily digest.
- Tapping a notification opens the relevant note or site, even if the app was closed.

## Settings

Inspectors can turn off each notification type individually. Supervisors cannot override those settings.

## Open questions

Whether "sync stuck" should also email the inspector's supervisor.

title: Larkspur: Customer Search Autocomplete
content:
# Larkspur: Customer Search Autocomplete

**Project:** Larkspur, the customer search box in the support admin console.

## Problem

Support agents find customers by typing an email address, name or order number into a search box that only runs when they press Enter and takes about two seconds. Agents run 40 to 60 searches an hour.

## Proposal

Suggest matching customers as the agent types.

- Start suggesting after 2 characters.
- Debounce keystrokes by 150 ms so we send one request per pause, not one per key.
- Show at most 8 suggestions: name, email, and most recent order number.
- Order numbers are matched by exact prefix; names and emails by prefix on each word.

## Backend

A dedicated prefix index over name, email and order number, rebuilt incrementally from the change stream. Target p95 latency: 80 ms per suggestion request. The existing full search stays behind the Enter key for anything the suggestions do not cover.

## Privacy

Suggestions only show fields the agent is already allowed to see, and every opened suggestion is logged exactly like a normal search.

## Success measure

Median time from starting to type to opening the right customer record drops from 9 seconds to under 4.

title: Public API Rate Limiting
content:
# Public API Rate Limiting

## Why

A handful of integrations send bursts of thousands of requests per minute, degrading the API for everyone else.

## Design

Limits are enforced per API key with a token bucket at the gateway.

| Plan | Sustained rate | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| Free | 60 requests per minute | 120 |
| Standard | 600 requests per minute | 1,200 |
| Enterprise | negotiated | negotiated |

When the bucket is empty the gateway responds with **HTTP 429 Too Many Requests** and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Every response carries `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset` so clients can slow down before they hit the limit.

## Exclusions

Health checks and the token endpoint are not rate limited. Webhook deliveries from us to customers are not affected.

## Rollout

Two weeks in report-only mode (headers sent, no 429s), then enforcement for Free, then Standard. Customers who would have been limited during report-only mode are contacted first.

title: Bulk Export to CSV
content:
# Bulk Export to CSV

## Problem

Customers with more than 10,000 orders cannot export them from the dashboard: the synchronous export times out after 30 seconds.

## Proposal

Make large exports asynchronous.

1. The customer picks filters and columns and clicks Export.
2. We create an export job and show it in an Exports list with its status.
3. A worker streams matching rows into a CSV file in object storage, in pages of 5,000.
4. When the file is ready the customer gets an email and an in-app notice with a download link.

## Details

- Download links are presigned URLs valid for 7 days; after that the file is deleted.
- Files are UTF-8 with a byte-order mark so spreadsheet tools open accented names correctly.
- At most 3 export jobs per account run at once; more are queued.
- Exports over 2 million rows are split into several files in one zip archive.

## Out of scope

Scheduled recurring exports and formats other than CSV.

title: Single Sign-On (SSO) with SAML
content:
# Single Sign-On (SSO) with SAML

## Summary

Enterprise customers want their staff to sign in with their company identity provider (IdP) rather than a separate password. We will support single sign-on (SSO) using SAML 2.0 for the Enterprise plan.

## Configuration

An account administrator enters the IdP metadata URL (or uploads the metadata XML) in the security settings. We show our entity ID and assertion consumer service URL to copy into the IdP. A test button runs a sign-in without enforcing SSO for anyone.

## Behaviour

- Users are matched on email address. The email domain must be verified by DNS record before SSO can be enforced.
- Just-in-time (JIT) provisioning creates a user on first SSO sign-in, with the default role for the account.
- When SSO is enforced, password sign-in is disabled for everyone in the domain except two break-glass administrator accounts.
- Sessions last 12 hours, after which the user is sent back to the IdP.

## Not included

SCIM user provisioning and OpenID Connect are separate follow-up projects.

title: Paid Time Off (PTO) Policy
content:
# Paid Time Off (PTO) Policy

This policy covers paid time off (PTO) for all permanent employees of Bluefen Systems.

## Entitlement

- Full-time employees receive 25 days of PTO per calendar year. Part-time employees receive a pro-rata share.
- Public holidays in your country of employment are additional and do not count against PTO.
- In your first year, PTO accrues monthly from your start date.

## Requesting PTO

Request PTO in the HR system at least two weeks ahead for anything longer than three days, and at least two working days ahead for shorter absences. Your manager approves or declines within five working days. Do not book non-refundable travel before approval.

## Carry-over

You may carry over up to 5 unused PTO days into the next calendar year. Carried-over days must be used by 31 March, after which they expire. Unused days beyond those 5 are not paid out, except where local law requires it.

## Sickness

Sick days are not PTO. See the separate sickness absence procedure.

## Leaving the company

When you leave, accrued but unused PTO for the current year is paid out with your final salary.

title: Parental Leave Policy
content:
# Parental Leave Policy

## Who it covers

All employees with at least six months of service who become a parent through birth, adoption or surrogacy.

## Leave

- **Primary caregivers:** 16 weeks of leave at full pay.
- **Secondary caregivers:** 6 weeks of leave at full pay, to be taken within the first year.
- Leave can be split into up to three blocks.

Parental leave is separate from paid time off; PTO continues to accrue during parental leave.

## Notice

Tell your manager and HR at least eight weeks before the leave starts, or as soon as possible for adoption.

## Returning

You may return on a reduced schedule (for example four days a week) for up to eight weeks at full pay. Your role is kept open for you.

title: Expense Reimbursement Policy
content:
# Expense Reimbursement Policy

## Principle

Spend company money as if it were your own. Costs necessarily incurred for work are reimbursed; personal costs are not.

## How to claim

- Submit each claim in the finance portal with an itemised receipt (a photo is fine).
- Claims must be submitted **within 30 days** of the expense. The portal rejects older claims automatically.
- Claims over €500 need your manager's approval before they are paid.
- Reimbursements are paid with the next monthly salary run.

## Meals and daily allowances

When you are away overnight for work, you may claim meals up to a per diem of €45 per day domestically and €60 per day abroad, instead of itemising each meal. Client dinners are itemised and need the attendees listed.

## Local transport

Taxis and ride-hailing are fine between 22:00 and 06:00, when carrying equipment, or when public transport would take more than twice as long. Otherwise use public transport.

## Not reimbursed

Alcohol unless at a client dinner, traffic and parking fines, upgrades to business class not approved in advance, and personal entertainment.

## Equipment

Anything over €200 is bought through IT, not expensed.

title: Information Security Policy: Credentials and Secrets
content:
# Information Security Policy: Credentials and Secrets

This section of the information security policy covers passwords, multi-factor authentication and machine credentials such as API keys and database passwords.

## Passwords

- Use the company password manager for every work account. Do not reuse passwords.
- Minimum 14 characters for any password you choose yourself.
- Never share a password in chat or email; use a shared vault entry.

## Multi-factor authentication (MFA)

MFA is required for email, the code repository, the cloud console and the finance portal. Hardware security keys are preferred; authenticator apps are acceptable; SMS is not.

## Machine credentials

API keys, service account tokens and database passwords are secrets and must live only in the secret store, never in a repository, a ticket or a chat message.

Every API key must be rotated at least every 90 days, and immediately if it may have been exposed. To rotate an API key:

1. Create a new key in the developer console with the same scopes.
2. Put the new key in the secret store under the same name; services pick it up on their next restart or within 10 minutes for services that reload secrets.
3. Confirm in the console's usage view that traffic has moved to the new key.
4. Revoke the old key. Do not leave it active "just in case".

Keys that have not been used for 30 days are revoked automatically.

## Reporting

If you suspect a credential has leaked, report it in #security immediately. Rotating first and asking questions later is always the right call.

title: Remote and Hybrid Work Guidelines

title: Weeknight Sourdough Loaf
content:
# Weeknight Sourdough Loaf

A loaf you can fit around a working day: mix in the evening, shape the next evening, bake the morning after.

## Ingredients

- 100 g active starter (fed 6 to 8 hours earlier) for the levain
- 400 g strong white flour, 100 g wholemeal flour
- 390 g water (78 percent hydration)
- 10 g salt

## Method

1. **Levain.** Mix the starter with 50 g flour and 50 g water in the morning. It is ready when it has doubled and a spoonful floats.
2. **Mix.** In the evening, combine the flours and 360 g water. Rest 45 minutes, then add the levain, salt and the remaining water.
3. **Bulk fermentation.** Four sets of stretch and folds, 30 minutes apart, then leave it. At 24 °C bulk takes 4 to 5 hours; stop when the dough has grown by about half and is domed and jiggly. Colder kitchens need longer.
4. **Shape.** Pre-shape into a round, rest 20 minutes, then shape tightly and place seam-up in a floured banneton.
5. **Cold retard.** Into the fridge overnight, up to 36 hours.
6. **Bake.** Preheat a Dutch oven at 250 °C for 45 minutes. Bake 20 minutes lid on, then 25 minutes lid off at 230 °C.

Let it cool for at least an hour before cutting.

title: Rosemary Focaccia
content:
# Rosemary Focaccia

Easy, forgiving, and better the day you make it.

## Ingredients

- 500 g bread flour
- 400 g lukewarm water
- 7 g instant yeast
- 10 g salt
- 60 ml olive oil, plus more for the tin
- 2 sprigs rosemary, flaky salt

## Method

1. Mix flour, water, yeast and salt until no dry flour remains. Cover and leave 30 minutes.
2. Do two sets of stretch and folds in the bowl, 30 minutes apart.
3. Cover and refrigerate overnight (12 to 24 hours). The cold rise gives much better flavour than a same-day dough.
4. Pour 30 ml oil into a 23 x 33 cm tin, tip in the dough, and leave it at room temperature for 3 to 4 hours until it fills the tin and is full of bubbles.
5. Drizzle the rest of the oil, dimple firmly with oiled fingers, scatter rosemary and flaky salt.
6. Bake at 230 °C for 22 to 25 minutes until deep golden.

Cool on a rack so the base stays crisp.

title: Lemon Tart with Brown Butter Crust
content:
# Lemon Tart with Brown Butter Crust

My sister Kate's recipe; the brown butter in the pastry is her trick.

## Crust

- 115 g butter, browned until it smells nutty, then cooled until just set
- 180 g plain flour, 40 g icing sugar, pinch of salt, 1 egg yolk

Rub the cooled brown butter into the dry ingredients, add the yolk and bring together. Press into a 23 cm tart tin, chill 30 minutes, then blind bake at 180 °C for 15 minutes with baking beans and 10 minutes without.

## Filling

- 4 eggs, 150 g caster sugar
- finely grated zest of 2 lemons, 150 ml lemon juice
- 150 ml double cream

Whisk eggs and sugar, add zest, juice and cream. Rest 10 minutes, skim the foam, and pour into the warm crust. Bake at 150 °C for 25 to 30 minutes until just set with a slight wobble in the centre. Cool completely before slicing and dust with icing sugar.

title: Chickpea and Spinach Curry
content:
# Chickpea and Spinach Curry

A pantry dinner in 30 minutes. Serves four.

## Ingredients

- 2 tins chickpeas, drained
- 1 onion, 3 garlic cloves, a thumb of ginger
- 2 tbsp curry paste or 1 tbsp garam masala plus 1 tsp each cumin and turmeric
- 1 tin chopped tomatoes
- 1 tin coconut milk
- 200 g baby spinach
- juice of half a lime, fresh coriander

## Method

1. Soften the finely chopped onion in oil for 8 minutes. Add garlic and ginger for one minute more.
2. Add the spices or paste and fry for a minute until fragrant.
3. Add tomatoes, coconut milk and chickpeas. Simmer 15 minutes until thickened, crushing a few chickpeas against the pan to thicken the sauce.
4. Stir in the spinach a handful at a time until wilted.
5. Season, add lime juice and coriander.

Serve with rice or flatbread. Keeps for three days in the fridge and freezes well.

title: Cold Brew Coffee Ratio
content:
# Cold Brew Coffee Ratio

1 part coarse ground coffee to 8 parts cold water by weight. Steep 16 hours in the fridge, strain through a paper filter. Dilute 1:1 with milk or water to serve. Keeps a week.

title: Red Wine Braised Short Ribs
content:
# Red Wine Braised Short Ribs

Worth the time for a Sunday dinner. Serves four.

## Ingredients

- 1.5 kg bone-in beef short ribs
- 2 onions, 2 carrots, 2 celery sticks
- 4 garlic cloves, 2 tbsp tomato paste
- 500 ml red wine, 500 ml beef stock
- thyme, 2 bay leaves

## Method

1. Season the short ribs well and brown them in batches in a heavy Dutch oven. Do not crowd the pot. Set aside.
2. Soften the chopped vegetables in the fat, add garlic and tomato paste and cook for two minutes.
3. Pour in the wine and reduce by half, scraping up the browned bits.
4. Return the ribs, add stock and herbs; the liquid should come most of the way up the meat.
5. Cover and braise in the oven at 160 °C for 3 hours, until the meat is falling off the bone.
6. Lift out the ribs, skim the fat, and reduce the sauce on the hob until glossy.

Better the next day: chill overnight, lift off the solid fat, and reheat gently. Serve with mashed potatoes or polenta.

title: Lisbon, May 2023
content:
# Lisbon, May 2023

Five days in Lisbon, staying with my friend Elizabeth Corwynne in her flat in Graça.

## Days 1 and 2

Walked everything. The hills are brutal in the afternoon heat; do the climbs in the morning. Tram 28 is charming but packed with tourists by 10:00, so we rode it at 8:00 from Martim Moniz and had it nearly to ourselves. Best meal was grilled sardines at a tiny place near the church where Elizabeth knows the owner.

## Day 3: Sintra

Day trip by train from Rossio station, 40 minutes. The palaces are spread over the hills, and the bus between them has long queues, so we walked up to the Moorish castle through the woods and took a tuk-tuk down. Pena Palace was worth the queue. Book the timed tickets online the night before.

## Day 4: Belém

Pastel de nata at the famous bakery (the queue moves fast), then the monastery and a walk along the river. Cycled back along the waterfront path on hired bikes.

## Notes for next time

- Get a rechargeable transit card at the airport metro station.
- Many restaurants close on Sunday evening and Monday.
- Bring proper walking shoes; the pavements are polished stone and slippery.

title: Kyoto in Autumn
content:
# Kyoto in Autumn

Eight days in Kyoto in mid-November, for the maple leaves.

## Getting around

We skipped the national rail pass: it only pays off if you travel between cities a lot, and we did one round trip from Tokyo. City buses are slow and full in leaf season; the subway plus walking was faster. An IC card works on everything, including convenience stores.

## Where we stayed

Three nights in a ryokan in Higashiyama: tatami room, futons laid out while we were at dinner, a shared cypress bath, and a kaiseki dinner of eleven small courses. Expensive but the highlight of the trip. Then five nights in an ordinary business hotel near the station, which was fine.

## Highlights

- Fushimi Inari at 7:00 before the crowds, walking all the way to the summit (about 2 hours round trip).
- Tofuku-ji's bridge over the maple valley, the most crowded and the most beautiful.
- Eikan-do at night, when the leaves are lit up.
- A morning in Arashiyama, going early and leaving before the tour buses.

## Lessons

Leaf season crowds are serious. Start every day early, do the famous places first, and keep the afternoons for quieter temples.

title: Driving the Iceland Ring Road
content:
# Driving the Iceland Ring Road

Ten days in late June driving the Ring Road (Route 1) clockwise from Reykjavík, about 1,400 km plus detours. Midnight sun the whole time, which is wonderful for photography and terrible for sleep: bring an eye mask.

## The car

We rented a small 4x4 from a local company at the airport. A two-wheel-drive car would have managed the Ring Road itself, which is paved almost everywhere, but not the gravel side roads to some of the waterfalls.

### Rental cover

This was the most confusing part of the trip. The rental price included basic collision damage waiver (CDW), which limits what you pay if the car is damaged but still leaves an excess of around €3,000. On top of that they offered:

- Super CDW, reducing the excess to about €400;
- gravel protection (GP), because passing cars throw stones and windscreen damage is very common;
- sand and ash protection, only relevant on the south coast in high wind.

My own car policy at home does not extend to rental cars abroad, so I took Super CDW and gravel protection at the desk, for about €22 a day together. We did get a stone chip on the windscreen on day 6, and it cost nothing at return.

### Fuel

Stations are far apart in the east. Fill up whenever the tank is below half. Pay-at-pump machines ask for a PIN, so bring a card that has one, or buy prepaid fuel cards inside the station.

## Itinerary

### Days 1 to 2: Snæfellsnes and the west

A detour from the Ring Road onto the Snæfellsnes peninsula. Black church at Búðir, sea cliffs at Arnarstapi, and a long walk on the beach at Djúpalónssandur.

### Days 3 to 4: The north

Akureyri as a base. Whale watching from Húsavík (humpbacks, very close), then Lake Mývatn: pseudo-craters, the steaming vents at Hverir, and a soak in the nature baths, which were far less crowded than the famous lagoon near the airport.

### Days 5 to 6: The east fjords

The quietest part of the trip. Long, winding fjord roads with almost no traffic; slow going but beautiful. Seyðisfjörður is worth the mountain pass.

### Days 7 to 8: Glaciers and the south-east

Jökulsárlón glacier lagoon at 23:00, with icebergs drifting out to sea in the low sun, then the black beach across the road where the ice washes up. A guided glacier walk at Skaftafell: crampons, ice axes, and a guide who explained how far the glacier has retreated since the 1990s.

### Days 9 to 10: The south coast

Waterfalls every half hour: Skógafoss, Seljalandsfoss (you can walk behind it; bring a waterproof), and the black sand beach at Reynisfjara, where the sneaker waves are genuinely dangerous. Stay well back from the water.

## Accommodation

Mostly family-run guesthouses booked months ahead, with shared bathrooms in about half of them. Breakfast was usually included and generous enough to skip lunch. Two nights in a farm stay near Vík, where the owner showed us the lambs and lent us rubber boots. Campsites are everywhere and cheap, but in June the wind made us glad we had a roof.

## Weather and packing

Temperatures ranged from 6 to 15 °C, with rain on four of the ten days and strong wind on the south coast. Layers were everything: thermal base layer, fleece, a proper waterproof jacket and waterproof trousers, a hat and gloves even in summer. Hiking boots for the glacier walk and the waterfalls; the spray at Seljalandsfoss soaks everything. Swimwear for the pools and baths, which every small town seems to have. Check the road and weather websites every morning; they show closures and wind warnings for each stretch of road.

## Costs

For two people, ten days: car and rental cover about €1,350, fuel about €420, accommodation (mostly guesthouses) about €2,100, food about €900 including many supermarket lunches. Iceland is expensive; the supermarket saved us a lot.

## Would do differently

- Allow twelve days rather than ten; the east fjords deserve more time.
- Book guesthouses in the north earlier; the good ones were full by March.
- Skip the paid lagoon near the airport and use the nature baths instead.

title: Carry-on Packing List
content:
# Carry-on Packing List

The list I use for trips of up to a week with only a cabin bag.

## Clothes

- 3 tops, 1 warm layer, 1 rain shell
- 1 pair of trousers worn, 1 packed
- 4 sets of underwear and socks (wash in the sink)
- Walking shoes worn on the plane; light sandals packed

## Tech

- Phone, charger, 20,000 mAh power bank (cabin only, never checked)
- Universal plug adapter
- Noise-cancelling headphones

## Liquids bag

Toothpaste, contact lens solution, sunscreen, all under 100 ml.

## Documents

Passport, printed copy of insurance details and bookings, a second payment card kept separately from the wallet.

## Tips

Packing cubes make it much easier to live out of the bag. Put anything you need during the flight in a small tote under the seat.

title: Berlin: Data Infrastructure Summit Trip
content:
# Berlin: Data Infrastructure Summit Trip

Three days in Berlin for the Data Infrastructure Summit, a conference trip booked through the travel desk.

## Travel

Train instead of flying (just under 4 hours, so the travel policy required it anyway). Hotel near the venue in Friedrichshain at €165 a night, under the capital city limit.

## Talks worth remembering

- **Running Postgres on Kubernetes.** The speaker's team moved away from operators for their largest clusters and back to dedicated machines, mostly because of storage latency. Worth sharing with the platform team.
- **Vector search in production.** Mostly about index build times and memory. Interesting claim that most teams would be fine with brute-force search below a million vectors.
- **Cost of observability.** Their log volume grew faster than traffic; they now sample debug logs at the source. Relevant to our build runner disk issue.

## The city

Walked along the remaining wall section in the evening and had excellent dumplings in Kreuzberg. The venue was a converted power station, freezing cold; bring a jumper.

## Expenses

Claimed meals under the per diem; one team dinner itemised with attendees.

title: Pension Contributions 2024
content:
# Pension Contributions 2024

## Current setup

- Workplace pension through salary sacrifice.
- I contribute 5 percent of salary; the employer matches up to 5 percent, so 10 percent goes in each month.
- Salary sacrifice means the contribution comes out before income tax and social charges, so the effective cost of each €100 contributed is about €58.

## Plan for 2024

Raise my own contribution to 7 percent from April when the pay rise comes through. The employer match stays capped at 5 percent, but the extra 2 percent is still tax-efficient. Tom agreed this beats overpaying the mortgage while the rate on the mortgage is fixed below 3 percent.

## Fund choice

Default lifestyle fund, 80 percent global equities, gradually moving to bonds from ten years before the chosen drawing age. Annual charge 0.25 percent. Review once a year, not every time the market moves.

## Old pots

Two small pots from previous employers. Consider consolidating into the current scheme; check first for exit fees and any guaranteed rates that would be lost.

title: Mortgage Overpayment Notes
content:
# Mortgage Overpayment Notes

## The rules

- The fixed-rate deal ends in March 2027.
- Overpayments of up to 10 percent of the outstanding balance per year are allowed without an early repayment charge (ERC). Above that, the ERC is 2 percent of the excess amount this year and 1 percent next year.
- Overpayments can either shorten the term or lower the monthly payment. The lender defaults to lowering the payment, so the term has to be requested explicitly in the online portal each time.

## What I do

A regular monthly overpayment of €150, set to reduce the term, plus a lump sum each December if the annual bonus allows. Stay well under the 10 percent limit so no ERC applies.

## Is it worth it?

At the current fixed rate of 2.9 percent, the guaranteed saving is modest. Priority order agreed with my accountant: employer pension match first, emergency fund second, then overpayments. Revisit before the fixed rate ends, since a higher new rate makes overpaying more attractive.

title: Reading Notes: Sparse vs Dense Retrieval
content:
# Reading Notes: Sparse vs Dense Retrieval

Notes from a week of reading about how search systems find relevant passages.

## Sparse retrieval

Classic keyword methods such as BM25 score documents by term overlap with the query, weighted by how rare each term is and normalised by document length. Strengths: exact matches on names, codes and rare words; cheap; explainable. Weakness: no credit for synonyms or paraphrases. A query about "automobile" does not match a document that only says "car".

## Dense retrieval

Dense retrievers embed queries and passages as vectors and rank by cosine similarity. They handle paraphrase well but can miss exact identifiers, and their similarity scores sit in a narrow band that varies by model, so a fixed threshold that works for one embedding model is wrong for another.

## Combining them

Hybrid systems run both and merge the results. Two common ways:

1. **Weighted score sum.** Needs both scores on comparable scales, which they usually are not; keyword scores are often unbounded.
2. **Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF).** Each document scores the sum of 1 / (k + rank) over the result lists, with k around 60. It ignores raw scores entirely, so it is robust to scale differences, at the cost of throwing away how confident each retriever was.

## Evaluation

Measure with a labelled query set: mean reciprocal rank, recall at k and nDCG. Break results down by query type; averages hide the query shapes that got worse.

title: Summary: Sleep and Memory Consolidation
content:
# Summary: Sleep and Memory Consolidation

A summary of several review articles on what the brain does with the day's experiences during the night.

## Main findings

- **Slow-wave sleep** (deep sleep, mostly in the first half of the night) appears to replay recent experiences, moving them from the hippocampus into longer-term storage in the cortex.
- **REM sleep** (more common towards morning) seems to help with integrating new material with what is already known and with emotional processing.
- Sleep after studying improves later recall compared with the same period awake, and the effect is larger for material that was only partly mastered.
- Short naps containing slow-wave sleep give a smaller but measurable benefit.

## Practical takeaways

- Do not trade sleep for study time before an exam; the last hours of the night are when REM is richest.
- Study, then sleep, then review: spacing sessions across nights beats one long session.
- Keep a regular schedule; the benefit depends on getting both deep sleep and REM.

## Caveats

Many studies are small and use word-pair tasks in a lab, which may not reflect real-world skills.

title: Book Notes: Focus and Attention Residue
content:
# Book Notes: Focus and Attention Residue

Notes on a book about doing demanding work without constant interruption.

## Core idea

Switching from task A to task B leaves "attention residue": part of your mind is still on A, so performance on B suffers. Checking chat for thirty seconds costs far more than thirty seconds.

## Suggestions from the book

- Schedule long blocks (90 minutes or more) for demanding work and protect them like meetings.
- Batch shallow work such as email into fixed times of day.
- Keep a shutdown ritual at the end of the day: write down open loops so they stop nagging.
- Measure hours of focused work per week rather than hours at the desk.

## My experiments

- Two 90-minute blocks each morning with notifications off. Output on writing tasks roughly doubled.
- Batching email into 11:30 and 16:30 worked; batching chat did not, because on-call needs it.

## Disagreements

The book undervalues collaboration. Some of the best work on the team comes from quick conversations the book would count as distraction.

title: Survey: Cache Invalidation Strategies
content:
# Survey: Cache Invalidation Strategies

A summary of the caching patterns I compared before redesigning the product catalogue cache.

## Expiry-based

Every entry gets a time-to-live (TTL). Simple and self-healing, but readers may see stale data for up to the TTL, and many entries expiring together cause a spike of misses.

## Write-through

The application updates the cache at the same time as the database. Reads are always fresh, but every write pays for two updates and a failure between them leaves the two out of step.

## Write-behind

Writes go to the cache first and are flushed to the database asynchronously. Fast, but data can be lost if the cache node fails before flushing. Rarely worth the risk for business data.

## Event-driven invalidation

Changes in the database are published on the change stream, and a consumer deletes the matching cache keys. Fresh and decoupled, at the cost of running the consumer.

## Cache stampede

When a popular key expires, hundreds of requests miss at once and all hit the database. Fixes: a lock so only one request recomputes, serving the stale value while one request refreshes, or adding random jitter to TTLs so keys do not expire together.

## Decision

Event-driven invalidation plus a long TTL as a safety net, with jitter.

title: Paper Summary: How Long Habits Take to Form
content:
# Paper Summary: How Long Habits Take to Form

## The study

Volunteers chose one new daily behaviour (for example, a walk after lunch or a glass of water with breakfast) and reported every day for twelve weeks how automatic it felt.

## Findings

- Automaticity rose quickly at first and then levelled off, following a curve rather than a straight line.
- The median time to reach the plateau was around two months, but the range was very wide: from under three weeks to well beyond the study period.
- Missing a single day did not measurably slow things down.
- Simpler behaviours became automatic faster than complex ones such as exercise routines.

## Takeaways

- The popular "21 days" figure is not supported; expect it to take longer.
- An occasional missed day is fine; consistency over weeks matters more than a perfect streak.
- Tie the new behaviour to a fixed cue that already happens every day.

title: Caffeine Half-Life
content:
# Caffeine Half-Life

Caffeine's half-life is about five hours in most adults, so half of a 15:00 coffee is still active at 20:00. Cut-off for me: no coffee after 13:00. Cold brew is not weaker; it often has more caffeine per cup.
